disclaimer: EczemaDetect is a student machine-learning project, not a medical device. Its prediction is a pattern match on one photo and can be wrong; many conditions (fungal infection, psoriasis, scabies, skin cancer) can look like eczema. Use it to learn and to prepare questions for a clinician, not to diagnose or treat yourself.
red_flags: Yellow/honey-coloured crusts, pus, rapidly spreading redness, warmth, or fever (possible infection)
Painful clusters of punched-out blisters or sores on eczema, especially with fever (eczema herpeticum, needs same-day care)
Rash near the eyes, on the genitals, or covering a large part of the body
Sudden swelling and pain in one leg (rule out a blood clot urgently)
Open sores or ulcers that are not healing
Itch that disrupts sleep, or no improvement after 1-2 weeks of careful self-care
general_care: Moisturise at least twice a day with a fragrance-free cream or ointment; apply within a few minutes of bathing to lock in water
Keep showers short and lukewarm; use a gentle, fragrance-free cleanser instead of soap
Pat skin dry rather than rubbing
Wear soft, breathable fabrics like cotton; avoid scratchy wool
Keep nails short and try cool compresses when itch flares to reduce scratch damage
Notice and write down triggers (products, foods you suspect, stress, weather, sweat) to discuss with a clinician

Atopic Dermatitis.summary: The most common, long-lasting form of eczema. The skin barrier leaks moisture and lets irritants in, and the immune system over-reacts, causing dry, very itchy, inflamed patches that flare and settle.
typical_look: Dry, rough, itchy patches; red on lighter skin, darker brown, purple or grey on darker skin
Inner elbows, behind the knees, neck, hands and face (cheeks and scalp in babies)
Thickened, leathery skin where it has been scratched for a long time
causes: Genetics: weaker skin-barrier proteins (e.g. filaggrin); often runs in families with asthma or hay fever
Immune system that over-reacts to everyday irritants
Triggers: dry or cold air, hot showers, harsh soaps and fragrances, sweat, wool, stress, dust mites, pet dander, and skin infections (often Staph bacteria)
self_care: 'Soak and seal': short lukewarm bath, then thick fragrance-free moisturiser within 3 minutes
Moisturise the whole body at least twice daily, even when skin looks clear
Use fragrance-free detergents and cleansers; rinse clothes well
Keep bedrooms cool and use a humidifier in dry weather
Identify and avoid personal triggers; manage stress and sleep
medical_options: Topical corticosteroids for flares (strength chosen by a clinician for body area and age)
Steroid-free creams such as calcineurin inhibitors, PDE-4 inhibitors or topical JAK inhibitors
Wet-wrap therapy, phototherapy, or for moderate-to-severe disease biologic injections or oral JAK inhibitors
Antibiotics or antivirals if the skin becomes infected
Atopic Dermatitis.see_doctor_if: Itch disrupts sleep or daily life, the rash spreads or weeps, or there are signs of infection.

Contact Dermatitis.summary: A rash caused by something touching the skin, either an irritant that damages it directly or an allergen the immune system reacts to.
typical_look: Red or darkened, itchy or burning rash where the substance touched the skin, often with sharp edges
Blisters, oozing or crusting in allergic reactions; dry, cracked skin in irritant reactions
Hands, face, eyelids, wrists (watch straps), earlobes (earrings), waist (belt buckles) are common
causes: Irritant (most common): frequent hand-washing, wet work, detergents, solvents, cleaning products, friction
Allergic: nickel and other metals, fragrances, preservatives in cosmetics, hair dye, rubber/latex chemicals, some topical antibiotics, poison ivy/oak
Allergic reactions can appear 1-3 days after contact, which makes the cause easy to miss
self_care: Find and stop contact with the suspected product; wash the area with lukewarm water
Cool, wet compresses to calm itch and oozing
Use gloves for wet work and cleaning (cotton liners under rubber/vinyl gloves)
Switch to fragrance-free, preservative-light products and add one new product at a time
Apply a plain barrier moisturiser after washing hands
medical_options: Topical corticosteroids; a short course of oral steroids for severe or widespread reactions
Patch testing by a dermatologist to identify the exact allergen
Antihistamines may help sleep but do not treat the rash itself
Contact Dermatitis.see_doctor_if: The rash is on the face or genitals, is widespread, blisters badly, or keeps coming back without a clear cause (ask about patch testing).

Dyshidrotic Eczema.summary: Also called pompholyx. Small, deep, intensely itchy blisters appear on the palms, sides of the fingers and soles, then dry and peel over a few weeks.
typical_look: Tiny fluid-filled blisters, like tapioca, on the palms, sides of fingers or soles
Burning or itching before blisters appear
Peeling, cracked, painful skin as blisters dry
causes: Exact cause is unknown; more common with atopic dermatitis or hay fever
Triggers: stress, sweaty hands/feet, warm humid weather, wet work
Contact with metals such as nickel or cobalt (including in some foods), or a reaction to a fungal infection elsewhere
self_care: Soak hands/feet in cool water or apply cool compresses for 15 minutes, then moisturise
Do not pop or pick blisters (raises infection risk)
Keep hands dry and protected: cotton-lined gloves for wet tasks, remove rings when washing
Manage sweating and stress; moisturise right after hand-washing
medical_options: Potent topical corticosteroids (hands and feet usually need stronger ones)
Drying soaks (e.g. aluminium acetate) for oozing blisters
Phototherapy, newer topical treatments for chronic hand eczema, or oral medicines for severe cases
Treat any fungal infection; patch testing if a contact allergy is suspected
Dyshidrotic Eczema.see_doctor_if: Blisters are large, painful, keep returning, or show signs of infection (pus, increasing pain, red streaks).

Nummular Dermatitis.summary: Also called discoid eczema. Distinct coin-shaped patches that can itch, ooze, crust and be slow to clear.
typical_look: Round or oval, well-defined patches 1-10 cm across
Lower legs, forearms, backs of hands and torso
May start as small bumps/blisters that join, then weep, crust and scale
causes: Very dry skin, especially in cold, dry winter air
Minor skin injury (insect bite, scrape, burn) that sets off inflammation
Poor circulation and swelling in the legs; contact allergens (e.g. metals, fragrance); bacterial colonisation
self_care: Moisturise thickly twice a day; ointments work better than lotions
Use a humidifier in winter; short lukewarm showers
Protect skin from scrapes and bites; avoid scratching
Avoid fragranced products and wool against the skin
medical_options: Usually needs a medium-to-strong topical corticosteroid, sometimes under occlusion
Antibiotics if patches are infected (crusting, pus)
Phototherapy or other treatments for stubborn cases
Nummular Dermatitis.see_doctor_if: Patches persist beyond 1-2 weeks of self-care, weep or crust, or you are unsure. Ringworm (a fungal infection) can look very similar and needs different treatment.

Seborrheic Dermatitis.summary: A common rash in oily areas of the skin, linked to an inflammatory reaction to Malassezia, a yeast that normally lives on skin. Dandruff is its mildest form; in babies it is called cradle cap.
typical_look: Greasy, yellowish or white flaky scale on red or discoloured patches
Scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose, behind the ears, beard area, mid-chest
Lighter (hypopigmented) patches can appear on darker skin
causes: Overgrowth of / reaction to Malassezia yeast in oily skin areas
Triggers: stress, fatigue, cold dry weather, illness, hormonal changes
More common in infants, adults 30-60, and people with some neurological or immune conditions
self_care: Medicated shampoo with ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione, coal tar or salicylic acid; leave on 5 minutes before rinsing, rotate if one stops working
Use it on the face/beard area too (lather, wait, rinse) a few times a week
Wash the face daily with a gentle cleanser; avoid alcohol-based products
Soften thick scalp scale with mineral or olive oil before washing
medical_options: Antifungal creams or shampoos (e.g. ketoconazole, ciclopirox)
Short courses of a mild topical corticosteroid, or steroid-free calcineurin inhibitors / roflumilast for the face
Seborrheic Dermatitis.see_doctor_if: Over-the-counter shampoos do not help after a few weeks, the rash spreads beyond oily areas, or it is very red and sore.

Stasis Dermatitis.summary: Eczema of the lower legs caused by poor blood flow in the leg veins (venous insufficiency). Blood pools, pressure builds, and fluid leaks into the skin.
typical_look: Swelling around the ankles that is worse at the end of the day
Red, brown, purple or rusty discolouration, itching, scaling on the lower legs
Over time: thick, hard skin, and sometimes open sores (venous ulcers) near the ankle
causes: Chronic venous insufficiency: weak valves in leg veins (often with varicose veins)
Previous blood clot (DVT), leg injury or surgery
Excess weight, long periods of standing or sitting, pregnancy, older age; heart or kidney conditions that cause swelling
self_care: Raise the legs above heart level for ~15 minutes several times a day and when sleeping if possible
Walk and do ankle/calf exercises regularly to pump blood up the legs
Wear compression stockings, after a clinician confirms they are safe for your circulation
Moisturise daily with a plain emollient; protect legs from knocks and scratches
medical_options: Treating the vein problem (compression therapy, vein procedures) by a doctor or vascular specialist
Topical corticosteroids for itchy flares; wound care for ulcers
Antibiotics if cellulitis (spreading, warm, painful redness) develops
Stasis Dermatitis.see_doctor_if: Always worth a doctor's visit, since the underlying circulation problem needs assessment. Seek urgent care for sudden one-sided leg swelling with pain, open sores, or spreading warm redness.

Normal.summary: The model did not find a pattern matching the eczema types it was trained on. This photo looks most similar to healthy skin in its training data.
self_care: Keep skin healthy with daily fragrance-free moisturiser and sun protection
If you still have itch, rash or changes the photo may not capture (lighting, angle, early stage), take another clear, close, well-lit photo or see a clinician
Normal.see_doctor_if: You have symptoms despite this result. The model only knows 6 eczema types and cannot recognise other skin conditions.
